title: Europe: Get Satellites or Get Throttled
content:
European powers must urgently break Elon Musk’s near-monopoly over military communications. It won’t be easy. It won’t be cheap. It won’t happen fast. But it’s necessary to ensure no one man can repeat the trillionaire’s treatment of Ukraine in early October, when he throttled Ukraine’s access to the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems now central to its military operations.

Starlink is a commercial satellite communications service, with Starshield a more capable military version. Both belong to Musk’s SpaceX. Ukraine — and many other Western powers, for that matter — relies on them for an array of vital military functions. They connect troops to their headquarters and drones to their operators.

Overnight and without warning in mid-October, thousands of satellite terminals failed in Ukraine. Operators discovered that SpaceX had imposed a speed limit of approximately 160 kmh (100 mph) or slower. Above that speed, a drone couldn’t connect to its operator. Many of the faster drones, including interceptor drones that Ukraine uses to defeat Russia’s own attack drones, couldn’t function.

title: Beware a Balkan Chinese-Russian Cyber Danger
content:
When Bosnia and Herzegovina held general elections last month, it used biometric voter identification and ballot scanners — a reform widely praised for producing fast and accurate results. That’s a real achievement. But the region’s digital foundations remain fragile, and the region’s adversaries know it.

The Balkan chessboard remains checkered, torn between attraction to the European Union and to Russia, with China maneuvering for leverage. Bosnian nationalists, including separatist, pro-Russian Serbs, won the recent vote. But Serbs gave a pro-European student-led movement a clear majority in another October election, while Montenegro and Albania closed chapters in their EU accession talks. 

The cheapest way to shift the balance of power is to undermine trust in the ballot. For the region, cybersecurity is not a technical issue. It is a strategic one. Washington is waking up to the risk — but needs to increase its focus on digital dangers. The EU is already pressing for action but must also increase its scrutiny.

title: Canada’s “Associate” EU Membership Should Be Digital
content:
When European Union leaders traveled to Montreal this month for the EU-Canada summit, they launched a grandly named “Alliance for the Future,” proposing to make Canada an “associate member” of the EU. A key part of the plan should be digital.

Europe has already negotiated five Digital Partnerships with like-minded democratic countries. Japan was the first, inking a digital deal in 2022. Since then, the EU has established agreements with South Korea, Singapore, Brazil, and Canada. 

In Montreal, Canada and the EU agreed on a legal framework to protect data flows from localization barriers and decided that Canada could participate in the EU’s high-performance computing partnership. But the existing digital partnerships remain, fundamentally, non-binding talk shops.

The motivation behind strengthening the deals is clear: reduce reliance on the US and China. But reinforced digital partnerships with like-minded democracies must push back against strong protectionist instincts, while remaining open to new participants, including the US — perhaps through a revived transatlantic Trade and Technology Council.

title: A Tungsten Truce – Allies Cannot Compete for Access
content:
Maine-headquartered Elmet Group bought 4.99% of Vietnam’s Masan High-Tech Materials for about $125m on October 1. Alongside the stake, Masan agreed to supply and process about 1,250 metric tons of tungsten trioxide equivalent annually for at least eight years.

Alarm bells rang in Brussels, where internal European Union documents warned competition from partner countries could disrupt Europe’s access to Vietnamese critical minerals, Reuters reported. Masan is a key tungsten supplier to the continent, particularly Germany, and the immediate question is who will be served first if supplies run short.

The annual volume committed to Elmet equates to about 1,000 metric tons of tungsten metal. That is roughly a third of Vietnam’s estimated 2025 mine output. It also represents about 4.4% of broader European tungsten end-use demand in 2025, which Fastmarkets estimates at 28,700 metric tons of tungsten trioxide equivalent.1

Tungsten, about two and a half times as dense as iron, is used in missile components and armor-piercing ammunition.

title: How China Might Target US Midterms
content:
No research shows Chinese propaganda or disinformation playing a pivotal role in the midterm elections, particularly when compared to Russia’s aggressive attempts. Yet significant blind spots exist. If it desired, Beijing is well-positioned to shape political debate through the WeChat app and through Chinese AI models.

Rather than shifting control of Congress, Beijing’s goal would likely be to reduce the presence of known Communist Party critics, particularly those serving in the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. Created by Congress in October 2000, the Commission monitors Chinese human rights and rule of law.

Several competitive races feature Commission members, including former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio and current Commission Chair Dan Sullivan in Alaska. House races in Iowa and Virginia involve current Commission members Zach Nunn and Jen Kiggans. Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate in Iowa, is on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, another Congressional body critical of the regime.

title: Ukraine Needs Clear Rules and Safeguards for Private Intelligence Companies
content:
Ukraine is the Wild West for many private intelligence firms, and in some cases an overreliance on them has put Ukraine’s intelligence community in a vulnerable position. Yet, with effective oversight mechanisms, they could help accelerate Kyiv’s intelligence reforms.

Private intelligence firms collect and analyze information from open-source and proprietary sources to produce actionable intelligence for the strategic decision-making of clients, and their operations in Ukraine have introduced new technologies, intelligence, and analytical capabilities.

Colorado-based Vantor, for example, provides geospatial intelligence derived from high-resolution satellite imagery that can be used to map, monitor, and analyze military activity. Its information has been used to monitor the activity of Russian forces in Ukraine and document their war crimes. Another example is Palantir, headquartered in Florida, which uses an AI-driven data analytics platform to facilitate quick intelligence processing.

title: India Stall Opens in Central Asia’s Military Bazaar
content:
While attention mostly falls upon China’s inroads into Central Asia’s economic and security spheres, so undercutting Russia, India has emerged as a new seller of weapons as the region diversifies its military procurement.

In early October, Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed that India had exported its domestically developed Akash air-defense system to Tajikistan. The system can intercept aircraft, helicopters, and drones at ranges of up to approximately 25 km (16 miles). New Delhi also confirmed the export of the same system to Turkmenistan, which had previously been reliant on Russian- and Chinese-origin air-defense equipment.

Cooperation has also expanded in other security fields. In September-October, India and Kazakhstan held the Kazind-2026 joint military exercise involving approximately 60 military personnel from each country. This followed the India-Uzbekistan exercises, Dustlik-2026, held in April and a similar drill held with Kyrgyzstan.

title: CEPA Podcast: Who Is Really Winning the AI Race?
content:
The CEPA Podcast is a series of dynamic interviews, bringing together leaders and experts from both sides of the Atlantic to explore the most important challenges shaping our world today.

In this episode, tech policy expert Ryan Fedasiuk examines how the United States can understand and outcompete China in critical technologies. From artificial intelligence and semiconductors to robotics and batteries, these technologies increasingly shape national power. Fedasiuk breaks down what computing power is and why it has become one of the world’s most strategic resources. He also explores why China is beginning to worry about the safety of its own AI, and what the race for compute means for allies on both sides of the Atlantic.

Speakers:

  • Ryan Fedasiuk, Fellow, American Enterprise Institute

title: Russia: The Revolt of the Letter-Writers
content:
In the days around October 30, Russia’s Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Political Repression, at least 160 gatherings have been planned to commemorate and support prisoners of conscience.  

Most will bring people together, often after public readings of the names of victims of Soviet repression, to write to today’s political prisoners, of whom around 1,800 have been formally recognized, though the true number is closer to 5,000. The evenings will span Russia from Kaliningrad to Vladivostok, with events abroad in places as diverse as Seattle and Seoul.  

Organizers represent a broad range of communities, including supporters of murdered opposition leader Alexei Navalny, regional branches of the liberal Yabloko party, a feminist anarchist collective and a grassroots educational initiative which writes to jailed students and scientists. 

Solidarity with political prisoners has become a powerful shared cause for Russians in exile and those who remain in the country, drawing people into collective action, as documented in a CEPA report in June.

title: Germany’s Security Consensus Assailed by Left and Right
content:
Recent months have brought electoral success in Germany for three parties on the populist extremes that challenge the country’s current security and foreign policy, albeit for different reasons: AfD, BSW and Die Linke. Might they pose a challenge to eight decades of broad European security consensus? 

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose electoral support surged to record highs in the recent elections in the east German states of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Saxony-Anhalt, is pushing for a softer line on Moscow: its Bundestag caucus has called for German weapons deliveries to Ukraine to stop, and for sanctions on Russia to be rolled back as part of peace talks. AfD politicians have also been involved in controversies related to their travel to Russia.

title: Georgia – A Step Away From One-Party Rule
content:
Georgia’s Constitutional Court has begun hearing a lawsuit filed by ruling-party MPs to ban opposition groups. According to the official results of the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, four of the five targeted opposition forces received nearly 800,000 votes, or about 38% of valid ballots.

The implications extend far beyond these organizations. Legislation adopted in May 2025 allows the court to ban similar successor parties and requires it to rule on such cases within 14 days. Separate amendments permit permanent restrictions on the political participation of individuals “associated” with banned parties.

The aim is to strip the opposition of its ability to contest future elections. Bidzina Ivanishvili, Georgian Dream’s billionaire founder and the country’s de facto ruler, wants voters to conclude that no organized alternative to his rule exists, and that political change is impossible.

Even by Ivanishvili’s standards, the attempt to eliminate meaningful electoral competition marks an extraordinary low. The closest recent parallel, other than Russia, is Belarus’s liquidation of opposition parties in 2023 after it stole an election from the democratic opposition in 2020.

title: NATO – Stop Training for Yesterday’s Wars
content:
Ukrainian soldiers returning from NATO training programs in Britain or Poland sometimes discover that lessons learned abroad require immediate revision. The problem is not necessarily the quality of Western instruction, but the assumptions behind it.

Much of the alliance’s small-unit training still reflects conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, where Western forces enjoyed air superiority, technological advantages, and relatively reliable evacuation and resupply. Ukraine demonstrates what happens when these advantages disappear.

The modern battlefield has become almost entirely transparent, with reconnaissance drones, thermal imaging, electronic surveillance, and first-person-view (FPV) strike drones fundamentally changing infantry operations. Traditional squad formations, vehicle movements, and defensive positions can be detected and attacked within minutes.

Ukrainian units increasingly disperse into smaller groups, sometimes operating in teams of two or three rather than conventional squad formations. Concentration, once essential for command and maneuver, now creates vulnerability.
